title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents

paper.title: Model What Matters: Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling for Language Agents
paper.abstract: Abstract Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM ( D ecision- G uided S elective W orld M odeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model’s prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language model (LLM)-driven agents can complete tasks such as retrieval, question answering, and web operations through multi-turn interactions with environments. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a direct training mechanism for optimizing task objectives for such agents, enabling models to progressively improve action selection and task execution capabilities based on environmental observations and task rewards. In recent years, PPO, GRPO, and related methods have been widely applied to LLM reasoning optimization and agent training, achieving significant progress ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Multi-turn tasks such as retrieval, question answering, and web operations typically exhibit long-horizon dependencies: current actions change environment states, and state changes determine subsequent available environmental observations and feasible actions ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) . To make effective decisions continuously in such tasks, policies need to form usable representations of action consequences and environment dynamics. RL primarily optimizes policy behavior through task rewards; trajectory-level or outcome-level rewards typically only evaluate task success and do not directly supervise action-conditioned environment transitions ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . Therefore, models can learn which behaviors are more likely to obtain high rewards, but may not explicitly learn what environmental observations actions will produce and how these environmental observations affect subsequent interactions; the action-environmental observation relationships already recorded in rollouts are also not fully converted into independent training signals. World modeling methods provide explicit environment dynamics supervision for policies by learning subsequent states or textualized environmental observations conditioned on actions, thereby supplementing training signals that rely solely on task rewards. Recent research further combines this learning objective with on-policy RL: ECHO optimizes the policy objective while using environmental observations produced by actions in rollouts for auxiliary prediction; PaW further filters transitions to be included in world modeling training on this basis. For transitions included in joint training, both typically use their complete next observation as the world modeling target (Figure 1 left), enabling the policy model to learn environment dynamics during interactions beyond task rewards ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . This raises the question we focus on in this paper: within a single environmental observation, should the complete observation be treated by default as a unified world modeling target? Our core insight is that environmental observations do not inherently possess equal supervision value. An environmental observation may simultaneously contain key information that can influence future decisions or content unrelated to the current task; if the complete environmental observation is uniformly used as a supervision target, the model must bear the same auxiliary prediction pressure for this content. Therefore, we argue that only observation content valuable for future decisions should be retained as world modeling supervision targets. Based on this insight, we propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training method for text agents (Figure 1 right). DGS-WM first filters content with decision value from environmental observations through Decision-Guided Observation Selection and constructs them as world modeling targets; subsequently through Confidence-Adaptive Weighting, it adjusts auxiliary supervision strength based on the model’s current prediction confidence for retained targets. Based on selected prediction targets, DGS-WM constructs world modeling objectives to jointly train the policy model together with RL objectives. Given the same environment observations, typical co-training methods supervise all observation content equally as WM targets (left), while DGS-WM selectively supervises only decision-relevant content based on their support for future policy responses (right). Green highlights indicate selected content; gray text indicates filtered noise. DGS-WM first filters content with decision value from environmental observations through Decision-Guided Observation Selection and constructs them as world modeling targets; subsequently through Confidence-Adaptive Weighting, it adjusts auxiliary supervision strength based on the model’s current prediction confidence for retained targets. Based on selected prediction targets, DGS-WM constructs world modeling objectives to jointly train the policy model together with RL objectives. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We propose DGS-WM, an RL and world modeling co-training algorithm for text agents that implements decision-oriented observation selection and adaptive supervision strength control through Decision-Guided Observation Selection and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting. 2. We propose a core insight: the world modeling value of environmental observations is not uniform, and complete observations should not be treated by default as unified supervision targets. Based on this, we refine supervision granularity to within observations, retaining only content valuable for future decisions as world modeling targets, and adjusting auxiliary supervision strength through confidence-adaptive weighting. 3. We conduct systematic evaluation on multiple public benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and web interaction. Results show that DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements across different tasks, model scales, and RL algorithms; in contrast, full observation world modeling methods (ECHO) show unstable performance in some settings, sometimes underperforming pure RL baselines.

sections.heading: 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has become an important paradigm for optimizing LLM policies. Existing methods first revolve around policy updates and advantage estimation: PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) constrains on-policy updates with clipped surrogate objectives, REINFORCE-style methods ( Williams, 1992 ) and RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) reduce reliance on explicit value models through sequence-level returns and leave-one-out baselines, while GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) performs group-based optimization using relative returns from multiple samples under the same input. Subsequently, extensive work has improved the training efficiency and stability of LLM RL from aspects such as clipped objectives, sampling strategies, loss aggregation, and importance weights, such as DAPO ( Meng et al., 2024 ) and GMPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . For long-sequence and multi-turn agents, research further focuses on how to perform finer-grained credit assignment using sparse outcome rewards, including GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) based on episode/state grouping, SPO ( Li et al., 2024 ) based on segment-level advantage, and Tree-GRPO ( Li et al., 2025 ) that constructs intermediate process signals using structured rollouts. Compared to outcome-level rewards, process supervision provides finer-grained training signals for intermediate steps, but typically involves additional annotation, estimation, or data construction costs ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) . The method proposed in this paper provides auxiliary supervision for RL training through world modeling, requiring no additional annotations and can be combined with different on-policy RL algorithms (such as GRPO).

sections.heading: 2.2 World Modeling for LLM Agents
sections.text: World modeling methods for language agents mainly revolve around learning action-conditioned environment transitions, i.e., predicting subsequent states or textualized environmental observations based on interaction history and actions. Early work typically places the learned world model outside the policy optimization process, serving as an environment simulator or planning module for generating imagined rollouts, performing search, or conducting lookahead planning ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Building on this, the WM-to-RL staged paradigm first uses interaction trajectories to learn environment dynamics, future state prediction, or other environment knowledge, then uses the obtained world model checkpoint or representations for subsequent policy optimization; Early Experience ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and RWML ( Yu et al., 2026 ) represent the reward-free world model warm-up and the approach of first performing world model learning then task-success RL, respectively. More recent work places world model learning and on-policy policy optimization in the same training process, forming a policy-world modeling co-training paradigm ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . Under this paradigm, environmental feedback included in WM training typically directly uses the complete next observation as the world modeling target, without further distinguishing content within the feedback, making all content jointly bear auxiliary supervision. DGS-WM continues this co-training paradigm but consciously selects world modeling targets, retaining only feedback content valuable for future decisions for world modeling supervision.

sections.heading: 3 Methodology
sections.text: We propose DGS-WM ( D ecision- G uided S elective W orld M odeling), a policy-world modeling co-training method for language agents that introduces selective environmental observation prediction supervision during RL training. As illustrated in Figure 2 , Decision-Guided Observation Selection uses subsequent policy responses to select world modeling targets from observations, and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting adjusts supervision strength based on the model’s prediction confidence for selected targets. The resulting world modeling loss is jointly optimized with the RL loss to update the same policy model. Figure 2: Overview of DGS-WM. Complete trajectories provide RL signal; observations and subsequent responses are used for target selection; history, action, and selected targets are used for world modeling prediction, producing target-level confidence and weights; weighted world modeling loss jointly updates policy with RL loss.

sections.heading: 3.2 Decision-Guided Observation Selection
sections.text: Complete environmental observations typically mix decision-relevant information with task-irrelevant content. Full-observation world modeling (Eq. 2) treats all content uniformly as world modeling targets, forcing the model to exert equal prediction effort on both noise and useful information. This not only wastes model capacity but may also interfere with the policy’s learning of critical information. Our core thesis is: only environmental observations that hold value for future decisions merit serving as world modeling targets . To this end, Decision-Guided Observation Selection uses subsequent policy responses to select supervisory content from observations. We first partition environmental observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} into a set of candidate units. The partitioning follows a “minimal semantically complete unit” principle: for retrieval document feedback, we split at sentence boundaries to obtain single-sentence candidates; for structured webpage observations, we identify semantically complete UI blocks (e.g., product cards, core purchase information, interaction feedback) as candidate units. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B. Formally, we split the observation into m t m_{t} candidate observation units arranged in original order: 𝒞 t = Split ⁡ ( o t + 1 ) = ( c t , 1 , … , c t , m t ) . \mathcal{C}_{t}=\operatorname{Split}(o_{t+1})=(c_{t,1},\ldots,c_{t,m_{t}}). (4) For each candidate unit c t , j c_{t,j} , we retain h t h_{t} and a t a_{t} , replace the current observation with that unit, and use the sampling policy π θ ¯ \pi_{\bar{\theta}} to compute the average token log-likelihood of the true next response under teacher forcing: s t , j = 1 | u t + 1 | ​ log ⁡ π θ ¯ ​ ( u t + 1 ∣ h t , a t , c t , j ) . s_{t,j}=\frac{1}{|u_{t+1}|}\log\pi_{\bar{\theta}}\left(u_{t+1}\mid h_{t},a_{t},c_{t,j}\right). (5) We define s t , j s_{t,j} as the response support score . Intuitively, s t , j s_{t,j} measures the policy’s average token log-likelihood for the true subsequent response u t + 1 u_{t+1} given candidate unit c t , j c_{t,j} . A higher score indicates lower policy decision uncertainty conditioned on that observation unit, meaning the unit contains more information supporting subsequent decision-making. All candidate units are scored against the same true subsequent response. We perform relative filtering within each observation rather than setting a global absolute threshold. This is because score scales may vary significantly across interactions: some environmental observations have high overall information content, yielding high scores for all candidate units; others contain more noise, resulting in universally lower scores. Relative filtering adapts to the scoring scale of different interactions. Let μ t \mu_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} denote the mean and standard deviation of response support scores across all candidate units in the current observation. The retained set is defined as: 𝒞 t + = { c t , j : s t , j > μ t + κ ​ σ t } . \mathcal{C}_{t}^{+}=\left\{c_{t,j}\;:\;s_{t,j}>\mu_{t}+\kappa\sigma_{t}\right\}. (6) Parameter κ \kappa controls filtering strictness. The threshold adjusts with the score distribution of the current observation, making selection criteria adaptive to scoring scales across different interactions. If no candidate unit exceeds the threshold, we skip world modeling for that interaction. Otherwise, we concatenate retained units in original order to form world modeling target z t + 1 z_{t+1} : z t + 1 = Concat ⁡ ( 𝒞 t + ) . z_{t+1}=\operatorname{Concat}\left(\mathcal{C}_{t}^{+}\right). However, selecting target content alone is insufficient: for targets the model has already mastered, continued supervision at equal strength wastes training resources; for targets not yet mastered, sufficient learning signal must be maintained. Therefore, we further introduce the Confidence-Adaptive Weighting mechanism.

sections.heading: 3.3 Confidence-Adaptive Weighting
sections.text: Target selection determines what feedback content to learn. To avoid continued equal-strength auxiliary supervision on already-mastered targets, Confidence-Adaptive Weighting adjusts supervision strength for each target based on the model’s current prediction confidence. Using the target average negative log-likelihood ℓ t \ell_{t} defined in the previous section, we compute prediction confidence: q t = exp ⁡ ( − ℓ t ) . q_{t}=\exp\left(-\ell_{t}\right). (9) q t q_{t} equals the geometric mean of target content token conditional probabilities, reflecting the model’s mastery of predicting the entire target. We accordingly compute the adaptive weight: w t = stopgrad ⁡ [ ( 1 − q t ) γ ] . w_{t}=\operatorname{stopgrad}\left[(1-q_{t})^{\gamma}\right]. (10) where γ \gamma controls confidence weighting decay strength. stopgrad \operatorname{stopgrad} indicates the weight does not participate in gradient backpropagation; gradients flow through the target prediction loss to update the model. Each concatenated world modeling target corresponds to one q t q_{t} and one w t w_{t} ; all content tokens of that target share this weight. High-confidence targets receive smaller supervision weights, while lower-confidence targets retain stronger learning signal, thereby adaptively adjusting auxiliary supervision pressure according to the model’s mastery of the target.

sections.heading: 3.4 Joint Optimization
Datasets.
sections.text: We evaluate on three task categories: (i) Multi-hop QA : HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) , Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) ; (ii) Single-hop QA : Natural Questions (NQ) ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) , TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) ; (iii) Interactive Web Shopping : WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare three method categories: (i) Prompting methods : Direct Inference and ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) ; (ii) RL-only methods : Primary experiments use GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ; cross-algorithm experiments additionally use PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , and GMPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) ; (iii) RL-augmented world modeling methods : ECHO ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ) and our proposed DGS-WM, which augment the RL algorithms above with world modeling. ECHO uses complete environmental observations as world modeling targets, serving as a full-observation baseline against DGS-WM’s decision-value-guided observation selection. Cross-model and cross-algorithm results compare each RL algorithm alone with its ECHO- and DGS-WM-augmented variants.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: Single-hop and multi-hop QA use Exact Match (EM, %). Unless otherwise specified, single-hop results are macro-averaged over NQ, TriviaQA, and PopQA; multi-hop results are macro-averaged over HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle. In Table 1 , Trivia, 2Wiki, MusiQ, and Bamb abbreviate TriviaQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle, respectively. WebShop reports Success rate (%) and Score (0–100 scale).

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: Primary table experiments use Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B ( Team, 2025 ) ; component ablation uses Qwen3-1.7B. Policy models are fine-tuned via LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) with rank 32. For QA tasks, we use the Wiki18 corpus with E5-base-v2 ( Wang et al., 2022 ) embeddings and FAISS ( Johnson et al., 2017 ) for retrieval. The selection standard deviation coefficient κ \kappa and confidence decay exponent γ \gamma are set to 0.5 and 1.0 respectively; following ECHO ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ) , we set the world modeling auxiliary loss coefficient λ WM = 0.02 \lambda_{\mathrm{WM}}=0.02 . All reported results use greedy decoding for evaluation. Additional details are in Appendix A.

DGS-WM consistently outperforms the ECHO co-training baseline across all task groups. On Qwen3-1.7B, DGS-WM achieves 45.77% and 22.06% average EM on single-hop and multi-hop QA respectively, improving over ECHO by 1.45% and 4.35%. On Qwen3-8B, DGS-WM reaches 50.14% and 40.48%, improving over ECHO by 1.39% and 2.33%. On WebShop, DGS-WM achieves 43.20% and 47.20% success rates on the two models, improving over ECHO by 2.80% and 2.20%. Notably, full-observation world modeling (ECHO) shows unstable performance, sometimes underperforming the pure RL baseline GRPO. For example, on Qwen3-1.7B multi-hop QA, ECHO achieves 17.71% average EM, lower than GRPO’s 18.88% (1.17% lower); single-hop average EM also drops from 44.64% to 44.32%. This comparison supports our core thesis: through decision-guided observation selection and confidence-adaptive weighting, DGS-WM provides more stable and effective auxiliary world modeling supervision.

sections.heading: 4.3 Generalization Across Models and Algorithms
sections.text: Table 2 validates DGS-WM’s generalization advantages over the ECHO-augmented variants. We test three additional models (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-7B) under GRPO, and three additional RL algorithms (PPO, RLOO, GMPO) on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Across all 6 configurations, DGS-WM consistently outperforms both the corresponding RL-only baseline and ECHO-augmented variant. This demonstrates that decision-guided selective world modeling provides stable auxiliary supervision across different model scales and RL algorithms, outperforming full-observation world modeling. In contrast, the ECHO-augmented variants show inconsistent performance: for GRPO with Llama-3.2-3B or Qwen2.5-7B, they improve single-hop average EM by 1.95% and 0.79% over the corresponding RL-only runs; for GRPO with Qwen2.5-1.5B, the single-hop average EM drops by 0.70%, and multi-hop by 0.52%. sections.heading: 4.4 Ablation Study
sections.text: Table 3 validates the necessity of both DGS-WM components. On Qwen3-1.7B, we compare GRPO alone, its ECHO- and DGS-WM-augmented variants, and two DGS-WM ablations. Removing Decision-Guided Observation Selection (DGOS in Table 3 ) reduces DGS-WM to confidence-adaptive weighting on full environmental observations, essentially an enhanced version of ECHO; removing Confidence-Adaptive Weighting (CAW in Table 3 ) retains observation selection but fixes all selected target supervision weights to 1 ( γ = 0 \gamma=0 ). Full DGS-WM achieves 45.77% and 22.06% average EM on single-hop and multi-hop QA, outperforming all variants. Removing DGOS drops single-hop and multi-hop average EM to 44.45% and 20.31%, decreasing by 1.32% and 1.75% relative to the full method; this variant uses full observations with confidence weighting, and its performance still exceeds ECHO’s direct use of full observations, indicating that confidence-adaptive weighting can partially mitigate noise interference from full observations. Removing CAW drops single-hop and multi-hop average EM to 44.82% and 21.66%, decreasing by 0.95% and 0.40%, showing that adaptively adjusting supervision strength on top of decision-guided observation selection further improves auxiliary training effectiveness. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We address the problem of non-uniform supervision value in auxiliary world modeling for language agents. Our core thesis is that not all environmental observation content holds equal value for future decisions—only decision-relevant feedback merits serving as world modeling prediction targets. We propose DGS-WM ( D ecision- G uided S elective W orld M odeling), which uses Decision-Guided Observation Selection to select supervisory content from observations based on subsequent policy responses, and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting to adaptively adjust supervision strength according to prediction confidence. Across benchmarks spanning single-hop QA, multi-hop QA, and interactive web shopping, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements over different RL algorithms and model scales, requiring no additional teacher models or human annotations and introducing no inference overhead. Experimental results show that compared to full-observation world modeling methods that may introduce noise interference, selective world modeling provides more stable and effective auxiliary supervision. These results demonstrate that environmental observations in on-policy RL trajectories, after decision-guided selection, provide a simple and practical source of world modeling supervision for language agent training.

sections.heading: 6 Limitations
sections.text: Despite its gains across benchmarks, DGS-WM still has two limitations. First, observation units depend on environment structure: QA uses retrieval-feedback sentences, while WebShop uses page structure. How to identify meaningful units in complex or unstructured feedback remains open; adaptive segmentation based on semantic boundaries, information entropy, or attention is a promising direction. Second, the response support score estimates an observation’s decision value from the policy’s average token log-likelihood of the true subsequent response. It assumes that greater consistency with the true response implies greater decision support, but this is correlation, not causation. Counterfactual reasoning or causal interventions could help identify feedback that truly affects decisions.

sections.heading: Appendix A Implementation Details
sections.text: Our experiments cover two types of tasks: Open-Domain Question Answering and Interactive Web Shopping.

sections.heading: A.1.1 Open-Domain QA
sections.text: Open-domain QA requires agents to answer questions by interacting with an external retrieval system without pre-given documents. We train on a mixed NQ + HotpotQA dataset and evaluate on multiple benchmarks.

sections.heading: Training Data.
sections.text: We mix the following datasets for training: • Natural Questions (NQ) ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) : 79,168 training samples and 8,757 validation samples from real Google search queries • HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) : 90,447 training samples and 7,405 validation samples requiring cross-document reasoning From the mixed dataset (169,615 training samples in total), we perform stratified sampling to obtain 27,648 samples for RL training and 1,024 samples for validation. The sampling strategy uses two-level stratification: (1) at the dataset level, NQ and HotpotQA are sampled with weights 1:4; (2) at the category level, within each dataset, samples are drawn proportionally to question categories (single-hop questions for NQ, type and level for HotpotQA). This ensures that the sampled dataset maintains the same distribution of hop counts and question types as the source dataset.

sections.heading: Test Datasets.
sections.text: • Natural Questions (NQ) : 3,610 questions evaluating single-hop fact retrieval • TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) : 11,313 questions on trivia knowledge • PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) : 14,267 questions focusing on popular culture entities • HotpotQA : 7,405 questions requiring multi-hop reasoning • 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) : 12,576 questions requiring comparison of two entities • MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) : 2,417 questions designed to avoid shortcut reasoning • Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) : 125 manually constructed difficult questions

sections.heading: Task Setup.
sections.text: Each question allows the agent at most 5 turns to complete the task. In each turn, the agent can execute search[query] (retrieve relevant documents) or finish[answer] (submit the final answer). The retrieval system is based on the Wiki18 corpus (a 2018 snapshot of approximately 5 million Wikipedia articles), using the E5-base-v2 encoder ( Wang et al., 2022 ) and FAISS index ( Johnson et al., 2017 ) for dense retrieval, returning the top-3 documents per search.

sections.heading: A.1.2 Interactive Web Shopping (WebShop)
sections.text: WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) simulates a realistic e-commerce environment with 1.18M products and 12,087 crowd-sourced shopping instructions. The agent needs to browse product pages and complete purchases according to user requirements (e.g., “buy a waterproof blue backpack under $50”).

sections.heading: Training Data.
sections.text: We use all 10,587 instructions in the training split; 1,000 instructions are held out for validation and 500 for testing.

sections.heading: Task Setup.
sections.text: Each shopping task allows at most 15 steps to complete. The agent can execute search[query] (search for products), click[element] (click page elements), or buy (purchase item). Success criteria include: (1) purchasing the correct item; (2) item attributes (color, size, etc.) matching requirements; (3) price within budget.

sections.heading: Base Models.
sections.text: Our main experiments use Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B ( Team, 2025 ) as base language models. Cross-model generalization experiments further test Qwen2.5-1.5B , Llama-3.2-3B , and Qwen2.5-7B .

sections.heading: LoRA Fine-tuning.
sections.text: To achieve parameter-efficient fine-tuning, we apply LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) to all linear projection matrices in attention layers: • LoRA rank: r = 32 r=32 • LoRA alpha: α = 32 \alpha=32 • Target modules: Q, K, V, O projections and all linear layers ( all-linear )

sections.heading: A.2.2 Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters
sections.text: We use GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) as our primary RL algorithm. Key hyperparameters are as follows:

sections.heading: Batch Size and Sampling.
sections.text: • Train batch size: 144 • Rollout group size: 8 (8 independent trajectories per group) • Number of groups per rollout: 18 (144 trajectories total) • PPO mini-batch size: 72 • PPO epochs: 1

sections.heading: Temperature and Sampling Strategy.
sections.text: • Rollout temperature: T rollout = 1.0 T_{\text{rollout}}=1.0 • Validation temperature: T val = 0.0 T_{\text{val}}=0.0 (greedy decoding)

sections.heading: Optimizer and Learning Rate.
sections.text: • Optimizer: AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999,\epsilon=10^{-8} ) • Learning rate: 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} • LR schedule: constant (QA); cosine decay (WebShop, 25% warmup, minimum LR ratio 0.1) • Weight decay: 0.01 • Gradient clipping: maximum norm 1.0

sections.heading: A.2.3 DGS-WM Hyperparameters
sections.text: The core hyperparameters of our method are:

sections.heading: Decision-Guided Observation Selection.
sections.text: • Selection standard deviation coefficient: κ = 0.5 \kappa=0.5 • Threshold formula: τ t = μ t + κ ⋅ σ t \tau_{t}=\mu_{t}+\kappa\cdot\sigma_{t} , so a candidate unit’s response support score must exceed the mean by κ \kappa standard deviations; μ t \mu_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} are the mean and standard deviation of response support scores within the current observation

sections.heading: Confidence-Adaptive Weighting.
sections.text: • Confidence decay exponent: γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 (linear decay) • Weight formula: w t , j = c t γ w_{t,j}=c_{t}^{\gamma} , where c t c_{t} is the response confidence at turn t t

sections.heading: World Modeling Loss Coefficient.
sections.text: • λ WM = 0.02 \lambda_{\mathrm{WM}}=0.02 (consistent with ECHO)

sections.heading: A.2.4 Reward Function
sections.text: We adopt sparse binary reward signals for all tasks:

sections.heading: QA Task Rewards.
sections.text: • Success (exact answer match): R = 1 R=1 • Failure (answer mismatch or exceeding turn limit): R = 0 R=0 • Invalid action penalty: − 0.01 -0.01 per invalid action (applied to corresponding action tokens in per-action mode)

sections.heading: WebShop Task Rewards.
sections.text: • Success (correct item purchased with all attributes fully matched): R = 1 R=1 • Failure (no purchase, wrong item, or attributes not fully matched): R = 0 R=0 • Invalid action penalty: − 0.01 -0.01 per invalid action (applied to corresponding action tokens in per-action mode)

sections.heading: B.1 QA Tasks: Sentence Splitting
sections.text: For retrieval document feedback, we split at sentence boundaries using forward sentence splitting with the following rules: Split pattern: We use the regex pattern (?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z0-9"’\(\[]) , which splits after sentence-ending punctuation followed by whitespace and a capital letter or digit. Abbreviation protection: Common abbreviations (Dr., U.S., Mr., Mrs., Ph.D., etc.) are protected from splits by checking whether the period is preceded by these patterns. Single-letter protection: Single capital letters followed by periods (e.g., "A. Smith") are preserved as part of the same sentence to avoid breaking names or list markers. Each resulting sentence becomes one candidate observation unit c t , j c_{t,j} with metadata tracking its paragraph ID, rank within the paragraph, sentence index, and character positions in the original observation.

sections.heading: B.2 WebShop: Semantic UI Block Identification
sections.text: For webpage observations, we identify semantic blocks based on page type inference: Page type inference: We classify each page as one of: search_results , product_main , search_home , or done based on page structure markers (search results list, product details section, search bar, confirmation message). Semantic block construction by page type: • search_results page: Each product card becomes one block, containing ASIN, description, and price as a unit. • product_main page: Core purchase information (selected options + title + price + rating + "Buy Now" button) forms one block; product description paragraphs are split into sentences; customer review blocks remain intact. • search_home page: Search bar and category buttons each form separate blocks. • Feedback blocks: System messages (e.g., "Added to cart") remain as complete units. Fallback handling: For unrecognized page structures, interactive buttons remain as whole-line units, while plain text content is split into sentences using the QA sentence splitting rules.

sections.heading: B.3 Granularity Design Rationale
sections.text: The "minimal semantically complete unit" principle avoids two failure modes: Over-coarse splitting (e.g., entire paragraphs or full product pages): Dilutes response support scores by mixing decision-relevant content with irrelevant context, reducing selection precision. Over-fine splitting (e.g., individual words or tokens): Breaks semantic integrity, making isolated fragments uninformative even when the complete unit would support decisions. Our task-aware unit definitions balance these concerns: sentences preserve propositional content in documents, while UI blocks maintain functional coherence in interactive environments. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM ( D ecision- G uided S elective W orld M odeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model’s prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM)-driven agents can complete tasks such as retrieval, question answering, and web operations through multi-turn interactions with environments. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a direct training mechanism for optimizing task objectives for such agents, enabling models to progressively improve action selection and task execution capabilities based on environmental observations and task rewards. In recent years, PPO, GRPO, and related methods have been widely applied to LLM reasoning optimization and agent training, achieving significant progress ( Schulman et al., 2017 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2025 ) . Multi-turn tasks such as retrieval, question answering, and web operations typically exhibit long-horizon dependencies: current actions change environment states, and state changes determine subsequent available environmental observations and feasible actions ( Feng et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2025 ) . To make effective decisions continuously in such tasks, policies need to form usable representations of action consequences and environment dynamics. RL primarily optimizes policy behavior through task rewards; trajectory-level or outcome-level rewards typically only evaluate task success and do not directly supervise action-conditioned environment transitions ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) . Therefore, models can learn which behaviors are more likely to obtain high rewards, but may not explicitly learn what environmental observations actions will produce and how these environmental observations affect subsequent interactions; the action-environmental observation relationships already recorded in rollouts are also not fully converted into independent training signals. World modeling methods provide explicit environment dynamics supervision for policies by learning subsequent states or textualized environmental observations conditioned on actions, thereby supplementing training signals that rely solely on task rewards. Recent research further combines this learning objective with on-policy RL: ECHO optimizes the policy objective while using environmental observations produced by actions in rollouts for auxiliary prediction; PaW further filters transitions to be included in world modeling training on this basis. For transitions included in joint training, both typically use their complete next observation as the world modeling target (Figure 1 left), enabling the policy model to learn environment dynamics during interactions beyond task rewards ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . This raises the question we focus on in this paper: within a single environmental observation, should the complete observation be treated by default as a unified world modeling target? Our core insight is that environmental observations do not inherently possess equal supervision value. An environmental observation may simultaneously contain key information that can influence future decisions or content unrelated to the current task; if the complete environmental observation is uniformly used as a supervision target, the model must bear the same auxiliary prediction pressure for this content. Therefore, we argue that only observation content valuable for future decisions should be retained as world modeling supervision targets. Based on this insight, we propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training method for text agents (Figure 1 right). DGS-WM first filters content with decision value from environmental observations through Decision-Guided Observation Selection and constructs them as world modeling targets; subsequently through Confidence-Adaptive Weighting, it adjusts auxiliary supervision strength based on the model’s current prediction confidence for retained targets. Based on selected prediction targets, DGS-WM constructs world modeling objectives to jointly train the policy model together with RL objectives. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1. We propose DGS-WM, an RL and world modeling co-training algorithm for text agents that implements decision-oriented observation selection and adaptive supervision strength control through Decision-Guided Observation Selection and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting. 2. We propose a core insight: the world modeling value of environmental observations is not uniform, and complete observations should not be treated by default as unified supervision targets. Based on this, we refine supervision granularity to within observations, retaining only content valuable for future decisions as world modeling targets, and adjusting auxiliary supervision strength through confidence-adaptive weighting. 3. We conduct systematic evaluation on multiple public benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and web interaction. Results show that DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements across different tasks, model scales, and RL algorithms; in contrast, full observation world modeling methods (ECHO) show unstable performance in some settings, sometimes underperforming pure RL baselines. 2 Related Work 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for LLM Agents Reinforcement learning has become an important paradigm for optimizing LLM policies. Existing methods first revolve around policy updates and advantage estimation: PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) constrains on-policy updates with clipped surrogate objectives, REINFORCE-style methods ( Williams, 1992 ) and RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) reduce reliance on explicit value models through sequence-level returns and leave-one-out baselines, while GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) performs group-based optimization using relative returns from multiple samples under the same input. Subsequently, extensive work has improved the training efficiency and stability of LLM RL from aspects such as clipped objectives, sampling strategies, loss aggregation, and importance weights, such as DAPO ( Meng et al., 2024 ) and GMPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) . For long-sequence and multi-turn agents, research further focuses on how to perform finer-grained credit assignment using sparse outcome rewards, including GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) based on episode/state grouping, SPO ( Li et al., 2024 ) based on segment-level advantage, and Tree-GRPO ( Li et al., 2025 ) that constructs intermediate process signals using structured rollouts. Compared to outcome-level rewards, process supervision provides finer-grained training signals for intermediate steps, but typically involves additional annotation, estimation, or data construction costs ( Lightman et al., 2023 ) . The method proposed in this paper provides auxiliary supervision for RL training through world modeling, requiring no additional annotations and can be combined with different on-policy RL algorithms (such as GRPO). 2.2 World Modeling for LLM Agents World modeling methods for language agents mainly revolve around learning action-conditioned environment transitions, i.e., predicting subsequent states or textualized environmental observations based on interaction history and actions. Early work typically places the learned world model outside the policy optimization process, serving as an environment simulator or planning module for generating imagined rollouts, performing search, or conducting lookahead planning ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Building on this, the WM-to-RL staged paradigm first uses interaction trajectories to learn environment dynamics, future state prediction, or other environment knowledge, then uses the obtained world model checkpoint or representations for subsequent policy optimization; Early Experience ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and RWML ( Yu et al., 2026 ) represent the reward-free world model warm-up and the approach of first performing world model learning then task-success RL, respectively. More recent work places world model learning and on-policy policy optimization in the same training process, forming a policy-world modeling co-training paradigm ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . Under this paradigm, environmental feedback included in WM training typically directly uses the complete next observation as the world modeling target, without further distinguishing content within the feedback, making all content jointly bear auxiliary supervision. DGS-WM continues this co-training paradigm but consciously selects world modeling targets, retaining only feedback content valuable for future decisions for world modeling supervision. 3 Methodology We propose DGS-WM ( D ecision- G uided S elective W orld M odeling), a policy-world modeling co-training method for language agents that introduces selective environmental observation prediction supervision during RL training. As illustrated in Figure 2 , Decision-Guided Observation Selection uses subsequent policy responses to select world modeling targets from observations, and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting adjusts supervision strength based on the model’s prediction confidence for selected targets. The resulting world modeling loss is jointly optimized with the RL loss to update the same policy model. Figure 2: Overview of DGS-WM. Complete trajectories provide RL signal; observations and subsequent responses are used for target selection; history, action, and selected targets are used for world modeling prediction, producing target-level confidence and weights; weighted world modeling loss jointly updates policy with RL loss. 3.1 Problem Formulation and Auxiliary World Modeling In text interaction tasks, a language model policy π θ \pi_{\theta} generates responses and executes actions a t a_{t} based on interaction history h t h_{t} (containing task instructions and prior interactions). (3) 3.2 Decision-Guided Observation Selection Complete environmental observations typically mix decision-relevant information with task-irrelevant content. Full-observation world modeling (Eq. 2) treats all content uniformly as world modeling targets, forcing the model to exert equal prediction effort on both noise and useful information. This not only wastes model capacity but may also interfere with the policy’s learning of critical information. Our core thesis is: only environmental observations that hold value for future decisions merit serving as world modeling targets . To this end, Decision-Guided Observation Selection uses subsequent policy responses to select supervisory content from observations. We first partition environmental observation o t + 1 o_{t+1} into a set of candidate units. The partitioning follows a “minimal semantically complete unit” principle: for retrieval document feedback, we split at sentence boundaries to obtain single-sentence candidates; for structured webpage observations, we identify semantically complete UI blocks (e.g., product cards, core purchase information, interaction feedback) as candidate units. Implementation details are provided in Appendix B. Intuitively, s t , j s_{t,j} measures the policy’s average token log-likelihood for the true subsequent response u t + 1 u_{t+1} given candidate unit c t , j c_{t,j} . A higher score indicates lower policy decision uncertainty conditioned on that observation unit, meaning the unit contains more information supporting subsequent decision-making. All candidate units are scored against the same true subsequent response. We perform relative filtering within each observation rather than setting a global absolute threshold. This is because score scales may vary significantly across interactions: some environmental observations have high overall information content, yielding high scores for all candidate units; others contain more noise, resulting in universally lower scores. Relative filtering adapts to the scoring scale of different interactions. Let μ t \mu_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} denote the mean and standard deviation of response support scores across all candidate units in the current observation. The retained set is defined as: 𝒞 t + = { c t , j : s t , j > μ t + κ ​ σ t } . \mathcal{C}_{t}^{+}=\left\{c_{t,j}\;:\;s_{t,j}>\mu_{t}+\kappa\sigma_{t}\right\}. (6) Parameter κ \kappa controls filtering strictness. The threshold adjusts with the score distribution of the current observation, making selection criteria adaptive to scoring scales across different interactions. If no candidate unit exceeds the threshold, we skip world modeling for that interaction. (8) Complete observations remain in the original RL interaction context; filtering only determines auxiliary world modeling target content. However, selecting target content alone is insufficient: for targets the model has already mastered, continued supervision at equal strength wastes training resources; for targets not yet mastered, sufficient learning signal must be maintained. Therefore, we further introduce the Confidence-Adaptive Weighting mechanism. 3.3 Confidence-Adaptive Weighting Target selection determines what feedback content to learn. To avoid continued equal-strength auxiliary supervision on already-mastered targets, Confidence-Adaptive Weighting adjusts supervision strength for each target based on the model’s current prediction confidence. Using the target average negative log-likelihood ℓ t \ell_{t} defined in the previous section, we compute prediction confidence: q t = exp ⁡ ( − ℓ t ) . q_{t}=\exp\left(-\ell_{t}\right). (9) q t q_{t} equals the geometric mean of target content token conditional probabilities, reflecting the model’s mastery of predicting the entire target. We accordingly compute the adaptive weight: w t = stopgrad ⁡ [ ( 1 − q t ) γ ] . w_{t}=\operatorname{stopgrad}\left[(1-q_{t})^{\gamma}\right]. (10) where γ \gamma controls confidence weighting decay strength. stopgrad \operatorname{stopgrad} indicates the weight does not participate in gradient backpropagation; gradients flow through the target prediction loss to update the model. Each concatenated world modeling target corresponds to one q t q_{t} and one w t w_{t} ; all content tokens of that target share this weight. High-confidence targets receive smaller supervision weights, while lower-confidence targets retain stronger learning signal, thereby adaptively adjusting auxiliary supervision pressure according to the model’s mastery of the target. 3.4 Joint Optimization Decision-Guided Observation Selection (Section 3.2) determines “what to predict,” and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting (Section 3.3) decides “at what strength to learn.” The two components jointly constitute our Decision-Aware World Modeling Loss . At inference time, the model directly generates policy responses based on complete interaction history, requiring no observation filtering or confidence computation, maintaining the same interaction mode as standard agents. 4 Experiments 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets. We evaluate on three task categories: (i) Multi-hop QA : HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) , 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) , MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) , Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) ; (ii) Single-hop QA : Natural Questions (NQ) ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) , TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) , PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) ; (iii) Interactive Web Shopping : WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . Baselines. We compare three method categories: (i) Prompting methods : Direct Inference and ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) ; (ii) RL-only methods : Primary experiments use GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) ; cross-algorithm experiments additionally use PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , and GMPO ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) ; (iii) RL-augmented world modeling methods : ECHO ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ) and our proposed DGS-WM, which augment the RL algorithms above with world modeling. ECHO uses complete environmental observations as world modeling targets, serving as a full-observation baseline against DGS-WM’s decision-value-guided observation selection. Cross-model and cross-algorithm results compare each RL algorithm alone with its ECHO- and DGS-WM-augmented variants. Metrics. Single-hop and multi-hop QA use Exact Match (EM, %). Unless otherwise specified, single-hop results are macro-averaged over NQ, TriviaQA, and PopQA; multi-hop results are macro-averaged over HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, MuSiQue, and Bamboogle. DGS-WM consistently outperforms the ECHO co-training baseline across all task groups. On Qwen3-1.7B, DGS-WM achieves 45.77% and 22.06% average EM on single-hop and multi-hop QA respectively, improving over ECHO by 1.45% and 4.35%. On Qwen3-8B, DGS-WM reaches 50.14% and 40.48%, improving over ECHO by 1.39% and 2.33%. On WebShop, DGS-WM achieves 43.20% and 47.20% success rates on the two models, improving over ECHO by 2.80% and 2.20%. Notably, full-observation world modeling (ECHO) shows unstable performance, sometimes underperforming the pure RL baseline GRPO. For example, on Qwen3-1.7B multi-hop QA, ECHO achieves 17.71% average EM, lower than GRPO’s 18.88% (1.17% lower); single-hop average EM also drops from 44.64% to 44.32%. This suggests that uniformly supervising all environmental observation content as world modeling targets with equal strength may introduce decision-irrelevant noise, interfering with policy optimization. In contrast, DGS-WM consistently improves over GRPO across all settings: on Qwen3-1.7B, single-hop and multi-hop average EM improve by 1.13% and 3.18%; on Qwen3-8B, by 4.21% and 4.69%. This comparison supports our core thesis: through decision-guided observation selection and confidence-adaptive weighting, DGS-WM provides more stable and effective auxiliary world modeling supervision. 4.3 Generalization Across Models and Algorithms Table 2 validates DGS-WM’s generalization advantages over the ECHO-augmented variants. We test three additional models (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B, Qwen2.5-7B) under GRPO, and three additional RL algorithms (PPO, RLOO, GMPO) on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Across all 6 configurations, DGS-WM consistently outperforms both the corresponding RL-only baseline and ECHO-augmented variant. This demonstrates that decision-guided selective world modeling provides stable auxiliary supervision across different model scales and RL algorithms, outperforming full-observation world modeling. In contrast, the ECHO-augmented variants show inconsistent performance: for GRPO with Llama-3.2-3B or Qwen2.5-7B, they improve single-hop average EM by 1.95% and 0.79% over the corresponding RL-only runs; for GRPO with Qwen2.5-1.5B, the single-hop average EM drops by 0.70%, and multi-hop by 0.52%. With Qwen2.5-1.5B and the three other RL algorithms, the ECHO-augmented variants are also unstable: under PPO, single-hop and multi-hop drop by 0.47% and 0.94%; under GMPO, single-hop improves by 2.17% but multi-hop drops by 0.29%. The gray dashed line marks the ECHO baseline (31.02%). 5 Conclusion We address the problem of non-uniform supervision value in auxiliary world modeling for language agents. Our core thesis is that not all environmental observation content holds equal value for future decisions—only decision-relevant feedback merits serving as world modeling prediction targets. We propose DGS-WM ( D ecision- G uided S elective W orld M odeling), which uses Decision-Guided Observation Selection to select supervisory content from observations based on subsequent policy responses, and Confidence-Adaptive Weighting to adaptively adjust supervision strength according to prediction confidence. Across benchmarks spanning single-hop QA, multi-hop QA, and interactive web shopping, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements over different RL algorithms and model scales, requiring no additional teacher models or human annotations and introducing no inference overhead. Experimental results show that compared to full-observation world modeling methods that may introduce noise interference, selective world modeling provides more stable and effective auxiliary supervision. These results demonstrate that environmental observations in on-policy RL trajectories, after decision-guided selection, provide a simple and practical source of world modeling supervision for language agent training. 6 Limitations Despite its gains across benchmarks, DGS-WM still has two limitations. First, observation units depend on environment structure: QA uses retrieval-feedback sentences, while WebShop uses page structure. How to identify meaningful units in complex or unstructured feedback remains open; adaptive segmentation based on semantic boundaries, information entropy, or attention is a promising direction. Second, the response support score estimates an observation’s decision value from the policy’s average token log-likelihood of the true subsequent response. It assumes that greater consistency with the true response implies greater decision support, but this is correlation, not causation. Appendix A Implementation Details Our experiments cover two types of tasks: Open-Domain Question Answering and Interactive Web Shopping. A.1 Datasets A.1.1 Open-Domain QA Open-domain QA requires agents to answer questions by interacting with an external retrieval system without pre-given documents. We train on a mixed NQ + HotpotQA dataset and evaluate on multiple benchmarks. Training Data. We mix the following datasets for training: • Natural Questions (NQ) ( Kwiatkowski et al., 2019 ) : 79,168 training samples and 8,757 validation samples from real Google search queries • HotpotQA ( Yang et al., 2018 ) : 90,447 training samples and 7,405 validation samples requiring cross-document reasoning From the mixed dataset (169,615 training samples in total), we perform stratified sampling to obtain 27,648 samples for RL training and 1,024 samples for validation. The sampling strategy uses two-level stratification: (1) at the dataset level, NQ and HotpotQA are sampled with weights 1:4; (2) at the category level, within each dataset, samples are drawn proportionally to question categories (single-hop questions for NQ, type and level for HotpotQA). This ensures that the sampled dataset maintains the same distribution of hop counts and question types as the source dataset. Test Datasets. • Natural Questions (NQ) : 3,610 questions evaluating single-hop fact retrieval • TriviaQA ( Joshi et al., 2017 ) : 11,313 questions on trivia knowledge • PopQA ( Mallen et al., 2023 ) : 14,267 questions focusing on popular culture entities • HotpotQA : 7,405 questions requiring multi-hop reasoning • 2WikiMultiHopQA ( Ho et al., 2020 ) : 12,576 questions requiring comparison of two entities • MuSiQue ( Trivedi et al., 2022 ) : 2,417 questions designed to avoid shortcut reasoning • Bamboogle ( Press et al., 2023 ) : 125 manually constructed difficult questions Task Setup. Each question allows the agent at most 5 turns to complete the task. In each turn, the agent can execute search[query] (retrieve relevant documents) or finish[answer] (submit the final answer). The retrieval system is based on the Wiki18 corpus (a 2018 snapshot of approximately 5 million Wikipedia articles), using the E5-base-v2 encoder ( Wang et al., 2022 ) and FAISS index ( Johnson et al., 2017 ) for dense retrieval, returning the top-3 documents per search. A.1.2 Interactive Web Shopping (WebShop) WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) simulates a realistic e-commerce environment with 1.18M products and 12,087 crowd-sourced shopping instructions. The agent needs to browse product pages and complete purchases according to user requirements (e.g., “buy a waterproof blue backpack under $50”). Training Data. We use all 10,587 instructions in the training split; 1,000 instructions are held out for validation and 500 for testing. Task Setup. Each shopping task allows at most 15 steps to complete. The agent can execute search[query] (search for products), click[element] (click page elements), or buy (purchase item). Success criteria include: (1) purchasing the correct item; (2) item attributes (color, size, etc.) matching requirements; (3) price within budget. A.2 Training Details A.2.1 Model and LoRA Configuration Base Models. Our main experiments use Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-8B ( Team, 2025 ) as base language models. Cross-model generalization experiments further test Qwen2.5-1.5B , Llama-3.2-3B , and Qwen2.5-7B . LoRA Fine-tuning. To achieve parameter-efficient fine-tuning, we apply LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) to all linear projection matrices in attention layers: • LoRA rank: r = 32 r=32 • LoRA alpha: α = 32 \alpha=32 • Target modules: Q, K, V, O projections and all linear layers ( all-linear ) A.2.2 Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters We use GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) as our primary RL algorithm. Key hyperparameters are as follows: Batch Size and Sampling. • Train batch size: 144 • Rollout group size: 8 (8 independent trajectories per group) • Number of groups per rollout: 18 (144 trajectories total) • PPO mini-batch size: 72 • PPO epochs: 1 Temperature and Sampling Strategy. • Rollout temperature: T rollout = 1.0 T_{\text{rollout}}=1.0 • Validation temperature: T val = 0.0 T_{\text{val}}=0.0 (greedy decoding) Optimizer and Learning Rate. • Optimizer: AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999,\epsilon=10^{-8} ) • Learning rate: 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} • LR schedule: constant (QA); cosine decay (WebShop, 25% warmup, minimum LR ratio 0.1) • Weight decay: 0.01 • Gradient clipping: maximum norm 1.0 A.2.3 DGS-WM Hyperparameters The core hyperparameters of our method are: Decision-Guided Observation Selection. • Selection standard deviation coefficient: κ = 0.5 \kappa=0.5 • Threshold formula: τ t = μ t + κ ⋅ σ t \tau_{t}=\mu_{t}+\kappa\cdot\sigma_{t} , so a candidate unit’s response support score must exceed the mean by κ \kappa standard deviations; μ t \mu_{t} and σ t \sigma_{t} are the mean and standard deviation of response support scores within the current observation Confidence-Adaptive Weighting. • Confidence decay exponent: γ = 1.0 \gamma=1.0 (linear decay) • Weight formula: w t , j = c t γ w_{t,j}=c_{t}^{\gamma} , where c t c_{t} is the response confidence at turn t t World Modeling Loss Coefficient. • λ WM = 0.02 \lambda_{\mathrm{WM}}=0.02 (consistent with ECHO) A.2.4 Reward Function We adopt sparse binary reward signals for all tasks: QA Task Rewards. • Success (exact answer match): R = 1 R=1 • Failure (answer mismatch or exceeding turn limit): R = 0 R=0 • Invalid action penalty: − 0.01 -0.01 per invalid action (applied to corresponding action tokens in per-action mode) WebShop Task Rewards. • Success (correct item purchased with all attributes fully matched): R = 1 R=1 • Failure (no purchase, wrong item, or attributes not fully matched): R = 0 R=0 • Invalid action penalty: − 0.01 -0.01 per invalid action (applied to corresponding action tokens in per-action mode) Appendix B Observation Unit Partitioning B.1 QA Tasks: Sentence Splitting For retrieval document feedback, we split at sentence boundaries using forward sentence splitting with the following rules: Split pattern: We use the regex pattern (?<=[.!?])\s+(?=[A-Z0-9"’\(\[]) , which splits after sentence-ending punctuation followed by whitespace and a capital letter or digit. Abbreviation protection: Common abbreviations (Dr., U.S., Mr., Mrs., Ph.D., etc.) are protected from splits by checking whether the period is preceded by these patterns. Single-letter protection: Single capital letters followed by periods (e.g., "A. Smith") are preserved as part of the same sentence to avoid breaking names or list markers. Each resulting sentence becomes one candidate observation unit c t , j c_{t,j} with metadata tracking its paragraph ID, rank within the paragraph, sentence index, and character positions in the original observation. B.2 WebShop: Semantic UI Block Identification For webpage observations, we identify semantic blocks based on page type inference: Page type inference: We classify each page as one of: search_results , product_main , search_home , or done based on page structure markers (search results list, product details section, search bar, confirmation message). Semantic block construction by page type: • search_results page: Each product card becomes one block, containing ASIN, description, and price as a unit. • product_main page: Core purchase information (selected options + title + price + rating + "Buy Now" button) forms one block; product description paragraphs are split into sentences; customer review blocks remain intact. • search_home page: Search bar and category buttons each form separate blocks. • Feedback blocks: System messages (e.g., "Added to cart") remain as complete units. Fallback handling: For unrecognized page structures, interactive buttons remain as whole-line units, while plain text content is split into sentences using the QA sentence splitting rules. B.3 Granularity Design Rationale The "minimal semantically complete unit" principle avoids two failure modes: Over-coarse splitting (e.g., entire paragraphs or full product pages): Dilutes response support scores by mixing decision-relevant content with irrelevant context, reducing selection precision. Over-fine splitting (e.g., individual words or tokens): Breaks semantic integrity, making isolated fragments uninformative even when the complete unit would support decisions. Our task-aware unit definitions balance these concerns: sentences preserve propositional content in documents, while UI blocks maintain functional coherence in interactive environments.
